analytic.title: האפשר שנביא יחטא? (על בעית "עצמה אלאנביא" באיסלם וביהדות)

biblStruct.note: A comparison of the views expressed by leading Jewish theologians of the 10th and 11th centuries with those of Islamic dogmaticians shows that the Jewish authors rejected the orthodox Islamic view that the prophets were infallible due to their inherent disposition, or to special divine protection. They could not accept this idea because of its challenge to the doctrine of free will granted to every human being. Rather, they approved of the Mu'tazilite opinion that no man is by his nature immune to sin and error, but God who foresees the future actions of men would not select as his messengers people of whom he knows would not be faithful to their mission or otherwise disobey his commands. The sages of the Talmud and the Midrash, in conformity with the literal meaning of the respective biblical texts, have charged Moses with several sins, such as: attempting to escape the mission of redeeming Israel from Egypt imposed upon him by God; doubting God's omnipotence, and other failures. The prophet Jonah is presented in the Babylonian and Palestinian Talmud as a classic example of a Prophet endeavouring to suppress his prophesy and to run away from his mission. Similarly the prophet, Isaiah is accused by the Rabbis of having slandered the people of Israel before God. In fact, none of the prophets is credited by the Talmudists with complete sinlessness. However, Medieval authors, such as the Geonim, R. Se'adya, R. Samuel b. Ḥofni, the Karaite Yephet b. 'Ali, who were all strict adherents of Mu'tazilite theology, reinterpreted the respective biblical passages in such a manner that the perfect integrity of the aforementioned prophets was established. The Gaon, R. Samuel b. Ḥofni, a most pronounced Mu'tazalite, even dedicated a large chapter of the introduction to his commentary on Deuteronomy to the subject of prophetic sinlessness. The view that Moses and Jonah did not endeavour to escape their mission, contrary to the older talmudic opinion, is also found in both versions of the Tanḥuma. This is to be taken as additional evidence that both of these versions present later compilations and are not to be dated before the tenth century. The last chapter of the article discusses the views of R. Se'adya and R. Samuel ben Ḥofni with regard to the question whether angels are liable of disobeying God's command; there too the two Geonim appear as faithful disciples of the Mu'tazilite school.
